content.thinking:
Now I see the actual file. The issue is that a new `Lock` is created inside the function on every call (`lock = threading.Lock()`). This means every invocation gets its own lock, so no two calls ever contend on the same lock — the lock provides zero protection.

For the lock to actually protect against concurrent access, it needs to be shared across calls. The fix is to make the lock a module-level variable or a function attribute.

Also, `list(a.items())` and `list(b.items())` are used to create snapshots of the items, which is good for avoiding issues if the dict is modified during iteration, but the lock should be shared.

The fix: move `lock = threading.Lock()` outside the function to make it module-level.

content.text:

Fix: make the lock a module-level singleton shared across all calls.
